04Questions

Before you book

Is my date held when I send a request?

No. A request starts the conversation. Management may place a short provisional hold while preparing your quote; the date is secured once the agreement is signed, the deposit is received and management confirms.

What does the quote include?

The performance fee, travel, accommodation, production and any additional costs, tax where applicable, the total, the deposit and balance, the payment deadline and the cancellation terms.

How do I pay the deposit?

From your private booking page, through a secure South African payment provider. Card details go straight to the provider — they never touch this website.

Who sees my information?

Only the management team handling your booking. The public calendar shows whether a date can be requested — never who has booked it or why.

The Story

More thana performer

Artist, producer, founder, curator — and the architect of what comes next.

Zakes Bantwini

The music came first. What it builds is the next chapter.

Zakes Bantwini is a South African artist and producer whose work moves between the studio, the stage and the boardroom. Known first for the music, the next chapter is about what the music builds.

As a producer, Zakes treats a record as architecture — foundations, structure and space — and brings the same thinking to performance, film and the rooms where other artists learn their craft.

Under the banner of The Architect, that work is becoming an institution: a Festival to gather the culture, a Label to build artists, a Catalogue kept as a working archive, an Academy to pass on the craft, and a Community with a direct line in.

Biography pending management approval

01  Origin

South African, first and always.

Every scene starts somewhere specific — a city, a set of streets, a few rooms where people gather to hear what is new. The music was made here first, then carried outward.

02  The producer

A record is architecture.

Foundations, structure, space and light. The producer’s job is to decide what carries the weight and where the air gets in — at the console, in rehearsal and on stage.

03  Creative philosophy

Build the room, then fill it.

Good work is made with other people. The sessions that matter have the right people in the room, a clear idea of what everyone is listening for, and space for someone new to be heard.

04  Cultural impact

Measured by who it reaches.

Beyond the stage, the work shows up in crowds that sing back, in young producers who learn a craft, and in the communities that gather around the music.

The Architect

TheArchitect

The next chapter is an institution rather than another round of competition — built with the same discipline as a record.

01The arc

Artist to architect

  1. 01ArtistThe voice and the stage.
  2. 02ProducerThe ear and the console.
  3. 03FounderThe company and the team.
  4. 04CuratorThe line-up and the room.
  5. 05ArchitectThe institution that outlasts the work.

02  The idea

Build something larger than yourself — and leave the door open.

Five pillars, one institution. Each is designed to stand on its own and to strengthen the others: the Festival gathers, the Label builds, the Catalogue keeps, the Academy teaches and the Community carries it all.

03Five pillars

The institution

FestivalLabelCatalogueAcademyCommunity
01

The gathering

Festival

A home for the culture to meet — curated with the care of an album and the scale of a landscape.

The Festival is where the music meets its people at full scale: open ground, a stage built for the place it stands in, and a line-up sequenced like a long-form record.

It is designed as an institution rather than an event — something that returns, grows and gives other artists a stage worth playing.

Copy pending approval
02

The platform

Label

A label that builds artists the way records are built: with structure, patience and space for them to be heard.

The Label turns a producer’s ear into a platform for others — finding voices, shaping records and protecting the people who make them.

Its measure is the catalogue it helps other artists build, not only the one it releases under its own name.

Copy pending approval
03

The archive

Catalogue

The body of work, protected, findable and put to use — a working library rather than a shelf.

The Catalogue treats every release, session and photograph as part of one archive: documented, preserved and opened up to listeners, researchers and the next generation of producers.

Kept this way, a catalogue keeps earning — culturally and commercially — long after release day.

Copy pending approval
04

The handover of craft

Academy

What took years to learn, taught deliberately — production, performance and the business of music.

The Academy passes on the unwritten parts of a career: how sessions run, how songs get finished, how contracts are read and how artists last.

It is the pillar where the idea of The Handover becomes practical: knowledge given to the people who will carry it forward.

Copy pending approval
05

The movement

Community

The people who carried the music this far, given a direct line in — early access, first word and a seat at the table.

Community is the fan relationship made direct: an email list and an optional WhatsApp line, early access to tickets and releases, and a membership pathway as the institution grows.

It is built on explicit consent and a simple promise — only send what is worth receiving.

Copy pending approval

04  What comes next

The Handover — a beginning, and a continuation.

The Handover

The nextchapter

A story told in chapters — about building, and about who we build for.

II / IV

Chapter I

Every chapter begins in motion.

The work started the way all work starts: one step, then another, through rooms that were not built for you yet.

Movement is the first lesson. You keep walking towards the light at the end of the corridor.

Chapter II

Build something larger than yourself.

At some point the question changes from “what can I make?” to “what can I build that outlasts the making?”

An institution is architecture for other people: a festival, a label, a catalogue, an academy, a community.

Chapter III

A legacy is measured by who it equips.

The next generation is not an audience. They are the people the work is being handed to — producers, performers, curators and fans.

Every room built now is a room they will fill.

Chapter IV

Not an ending. A continuation.

A handover is the moment a body of work is entrusted to the people who will carry it — and the beginning of what they make of it.

This chapter is still being written.

Privacy notice

Your information

Draft — for review by management’s legal adviser

This website collects personal information only when you give it to us, and uses it only for the reason you gave it.

Booking requests

Your name, organisation, contact details and event details are used by management to review your request, prepare a quote and agreement, take payment and deliver the event. Uploaded event briefs are stored privately and opened only by management.

Payments

Card payments are processed by a third-party payment provider on its own secure pages. Card details are never sent to, or stored by, this website.

Community and collaboration

If you join the community, we keep your email (and mobile number, if you choose WhatsApp) with the exact wording you agreed to. You can unsubscribe or reply STOP at any time. Collaboration proposals are read by the team and used only to respond.

Analytics

We measure how the site is used (for example, that a booking was started) without recording names, emails or phone numbers in analytics.

Your rights

You may ask to see, correct or delete the information we hold about you by replying to any email we have sent, or through the booking team.

Live

The room before the stage

Every show is decided long before the lights come up — in a quiet room, with a jacket on a hanger and a table of cables.
Copy pending approval

Audiences meet the performance at its loudest. The work that shapes it happens at the other end of the volume dial: a dressing room, a running order, in-ear monitors laid out in a case, a pass on a lanyard.

Preparation is where a set stops being a list of songs and becomes an arc — where the opening is chosen for the room in front of it, and the close is held back until the room has earned it.

The stage is the last place the show is built.

It is also where a promise to a promoter, a festival or a private host gets kept. The booking may have taken weeks. The quiet hour beforehand is what makes it worth it.

Legacy

What an archive is for

A catalogue is not a shelf of finished things. Kept well, it is a working library for whoever comes next.
Copy pending approval

Records, tapes, photographs, contracts, notes in the margin. An archive is the evidence of how the music was made — and the raw material for what it becomes.

Treated as storage, it gathers dust. Treated as an institution, it teaches: producers learn arrangement from the sessions, writers learn structure from the drafts, and the culture learns its own history from the source.

Music was the beginning. The vision builds the legacy.

That is the thinking behind the Catalogue pillar of The Architect: protect the work, make it findable, and put it to use.

Studio

Build the room, then fill it

The studio is a room for other people as much as it is for the producer at the desk.
Copy pending approval

A mixing console looks like a single person’s instrument. In practice it is a meeting place: a producer, an engineer, a young artist with headphones on, each with a hand on a different fader.

The best sessions are built before anyone plays a note. Who is in the room, what they are listening for, how decisions get made — that is architecture too.

It is why the Label and the Academy sit beside the music in The Architect’s plan. A room that makes good records should also make good record-makers.

Culture

A festival is a promise

Open ground at sunset, a stage dressed in timber and cloth, and a crowd that travelled to be there.
Copy pending approval

A festival makes a promise to its audience before a single act is announced: that the day will be worth the journey, that the ground will be safe, that the music will be chosen with care.

Keeping that promise is curation — of artists, of place, of the order of a long evening. It is the same discipline as sequencing an album, at the scale of a landscape.

Curation is composition at the scale of a day.

The Festival pillar is The Architect’s way of building that promise into something that lasts beyond one weekend.

People

Teaching what took years

The shortest route through the music industry is someone who has already walked it, willing to draw the map.
Copy pending approval

Most of what a working producer knows is never written down: how a session runs, how a song gets finished, how a contract is read, how a career survives its first success.

An academy turns that unwritten knowledge into something passed on deliberately — in rooms full of notebooks, keyboards and questions.

The Academy pillar is built on that idea: that a legacy is measured by the people it equips.

Music

Sound is architecture

A track has foundations, load-bearing walls and open space. The producer decides where the light comes in.
Copy pending approval

Low end is the foundation. Rhythm is structure. The space between sounds is as designed as the sounds themselves — leave too little and a record suffocates; leave too much and it falls apart.

That is why “architect” is not a metaphor borrowed from somewhere else. It describes the job.

Build for the room. Then build the room.

Music

Directing the frame

A video is a second arrangement of the song — for the eye.
Copy pending approval

On set, the questions are the same ones asked at the console: what leads, what supports, what is left out. The answers are just made with light and lenses instead of faders.

Owning the image as carefully as the sound is part of building an artist’s world — and part of what turns a catalogue into a body of work.

Culture

The city after dark

South African cities hum on a frequency of their own — highways, towers and the sound coming out of every open door.
Copy pending approval

Every scene starts somewhere specific: a city, a set of streets, a few rooms where people gather to hear what is new.

Johannesburg at dusk is a reminder that global music is always local first — built in particular places by particular people, then carried outward.

The Community pillar starts here: with the people in the room, and a way to keep them close.

Next story

The room before the stage

Every show is decided long before the lights come up — in a quiet room, with a jacket on a hanger and a table of cables.

The vision builds the legacy.
